nameStory: This grass gets its curious name from its fuzzy, hair-like flower clusters that might remind you of a scraggly beard - though it's called 'false' bearded because the hairs aren't quite as prominent as in some other grasses. The scientific name 'mattamuskeetense' comes from Lake Mattamuskeet in North Carolina, where this species was first scientifically described.
description: False bearded panic grass is a delicate native grass that forms small clumps in wet meadows and shoreline areas. It typically grows 1-3 feet tall with narrow, soft leaves and airy flower clusters that appear almost cloud-like when they catch the light. Like other rosette grasses, it has two distinct growth phases - a leafy rosette stage in spring and an upright flowering stage in summer. This is one of the rarer panic grasses in New England, making any sighting special.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Delicate, open flower clusters (panicles) that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch, with tiny seeds that have short, barely visible hairs - the source of the 'false bearded' name

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, soft leaves that feel smooth when you run your finger from base to tip, but slightly rough in the opposite direction, typically 3-6 inches long

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms loose clumps rather than spreading runners, with stems that often lean or bend gracefully rather than standing rigidly upright

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny, smooth, oval seeds that are less than 1/8 inch long and have a subtle shine when examined closely

habitat: Look for this rare grass in wet meadows, marshy areas, and along pond or stream edges where the soil stays moist through most of the growing season. It prefers areas with some shade or partial sun rather than full blazing sunlight. In New England, it's most likely to be found in coastal plain areas and low-lying wetlands.

seasonality.spring: Young plants form neat rosettes of soft leaves close to the ground, easily overlooked among other emerging vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Flowering stems shoot up in mid to late summer, producing the characteristic fuzzy seed heads that make identification much easier.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and the whole plant begins to turn golden-brown, with seed heads becoming more obvious as other vegetation dies back.
seasonality.winter: Dried stems and seed heads may persist into early winter, appearing as delicate tan skeletons above the snow.

funFact: With only 4 recorded observations in all of New England, finding false bearded panic grass is like discovering a botanical needle in a haystack - you're more likely to spot a rare bird than this elusive grass!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other Dichanthelium species, but the combination of wetland habitat and very sparse, soft-fuzzy seed heads helps distinguish it. Many other panic grasses have denser flower clusters or prefer drier sites.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'panic grass' has nothing to do with anxiety - it comes from the Latin 'panicum,' the ancient Roman word for millet, as many of these grasses produce small, millet-like seeds that were once gathered for food.
compareHints: Unlike the more common deertongue with its broad leaves and dense shade tolerance, false bearded panic grass has much narrower leaves and prefers wet, open areas. It's also much less hairy overall than hairy rosette-panicgrass, and its seed heads are more open and delicate than the compact clusters of most other Dichanthelium species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the many Dichanthelium species in New England, deertongue stands out for its relatively large size (up to 4.
Starved witchgrass is much more delicate and sparse than its relatives like deertongue or broad-leaved panic grass, which have wider leaves and more robust growth.
Among its many witchgrass relatives, forked witchgrass stands out for its distinctly Y-shaped branching pattern.
Among its Dichanthelium relatives, broad-leaved panic grass stands out for having the widest leaves - most other rosette grasses have much narrower, linear blades.

Among its rosette grass relatives, round-fruited rosette-panicgrass is distinguished primarily by its perfectly spherical seeds - most others like hairy rosette-panicgrass or deertongue have oval or egg-shaped seeds.
Among its many rosette grass relatives, hairy rosette-panicgrass stands out for its consistently fuzzy, velvety texture - most others like deertongue feel smooth or slightly rough.
Among its witchgrass relatives, Bosc's witchgrass tends to have broader leaves than Starved Witchgrass or Slim-leaf Witchgrass, but narrower leaves than broad-leaved panic grass.
Among its many rosette grass relatives, Slim-leaf Witchgrass stands out for having the narrowest leaves - most other Dichanthelium species have broader, more oval-shaped leaves.
Among its many Dichanthelium relatives in New England, variable witchgrass tends to be more adaptable to different moisture levels than most.
Among its witchgrass relatives, Small-fruited Witchgrass is distinguished primarily by its exceptionally tiny seeds - much smaller than deertongue or broad-leaved panic grass.
Wright's Rosette Grass differs from its relatives like deertongue and the various witchgrasses by forming more perfectly circular, compact rosettes rather than loose clumps.
Compared to its Dichanthelium relatives, slender panic grass is notably more delicate and fine-textured than broad-leaved panic grass, and lacks the dense hairiness of hairy rosette-panicgrass.
Northern witchgrass is distinguished from its Dichanthelium relatives primarily by its northern range preference and smaller overall size.

Among the many panic grass relatives in New England, velvet panicum stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety texture - most other Dichanthelium species are hairy but not nearly as plush-feeling.

Among its many Dichanthelium relatives in New England, Heller's rosette grass stands out for its strong preference for partial shade rather than full sun, and its consistently neat rosette growth pattern.

Among the rosette grasses, Scribner's Panicgrass is distinguished by its relatively narrow rosette leaves compared to broad-leaved panic grass, and its more pointed leaf tips compared to the rounded leaves of deertongue.

Eaton's Witchgrass is distinguished from its many Dichanthelium relatives by subtle differences in leaf width, flower cluster branching patterns, and seed size - characteristics that often require expert identification.

Old-field panic grass differs from its many Dichanthelium relatives primarily by habitat preference - while species like deertongue prefer shady woodlands, old-field panic grass seeks out sunny, disturbed areas.
Among its many Dichanthelium relatives, old field panic grass is distinguished by its preference for truly open, disturbed habitats rather than woodland edges.
Among New England's rosette grasses, Lindheimer's panicgrass stands out for its nearly hairless leaves and preference for wetter soils.
Hemlock panic grass differs from its Dichanthelium relatives by its preference for coniferous rather than deciduous woods and its particularly delicate, narrow leaves.
